description: We are 'Ojo de Agua', born in the Andean Cloud Belt at Space Apps Ipiales for 'Dancing with the SARs'. We monitor high-altitude reservoirs through persistent clouds using NISAR radar (GCOV/SME2) and OPERA. Validated on Bogotá's water crisis during El Niño with official ground data, our platform provides a scalable blueprint for cloud-covered Andean watersheds across Colombia. Profile: satellite remote sensing, Python/GDAL data pipelines, MapLibre web mapping, and water resilience.
summary:
Bogotá recently endured 366 consecutive days of emergency water rationing after its primary reservoir dropped to 17.9% capacity. Monitoring Andean reservoirs from space is severely hindered by 82.9% persistent annual cloud cover (NASA POWER regional cell), blinding conventional optical satellites.

'Ojo de Agua' explores this barrier using NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band synthetic aperture radar (SAR) to penetrate clouds 24/7. Directly processing Level-2 GCOV backscatter in decibels (γ⁰ dB via NASA Harmony), our open-source pipeline tracks official reservoir storage from XM Sinergox (Spearman ρ = 0.9831, p = 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁵, n = 21).
details:
### 1. What problem does it solve?

Between April 2024 and April 2025, over 8 million residents in Bogotá and 11 surrounding municipalities were subjected to strict water rationing due to unprecedented drought during El Niño. The Chingaza reservoir system (Chuza and San Rafael), which supplies ~70% of the capital's drinking water, fell to record lows. In October 2026, Colombia’s meteorological authority (IDEAM) declared the official return of El Niño conditions.

The fundamental operational challenge in monitoring high Andean water resources is "optical satellite blindness": according to NASA POWER solar and meteorological datasets, the regional grid cell covering Chingaza averages 82.9% cloud cover year-round (and 87.3% in Ipiales). Traditional multispectral optical sensors (such as Landsat or Sentinel-2) are frequently obscured precisely when continuous observation is most needed during cloudy rainy and refill seasons.

### 2. How does it address the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge?

'Ojo de Agua' directly responds to the challenge by leveraging Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) from the flagship NASA-ISRO NISAR mission. Operating at L-band microwave frequency (~24 cm wavelength), NISAR's radar pulses pass unobstructed through dense cloud decks, haze, and rain, day and night.

Calm water surfaces behave as specular reflectors, scattering radar pulses away from the antenna and appearing as distinct low-backscatter dark pixels, in sharp contrast with the diffuse volume scattering of surrounding páramo and forest vegetation. Our platform applies an automated OpenCV processing pipeline to estimate reservoir water surface area across satellite overpasses.

### 3. How was it built? (Technical Architecture & Pipeline)

Our solution is built entirely on open-source, reproducible technologies without proprietary backend dependencies:

- Primary Method (Native dB Backscatter via NASA Harmony): Direct cloud subsetting of Level-2 NISAR GCOV (radiometric terrain-corrected gamma-0, γ⁰) via NASA Harmony OGC API Coverages (ASF DAAC) across all 21 overpasses in EPSG:32618. Converted to decibels (γ⁰_dB = 10 * log10(power)) and segmented using an adaptive Otsu threshold within an empirical 300m buffer candidate ROI derived from the real reservoir contour.

- Comparison Series (NASA GIBS WMTS): Parallel time series using the NASA GIBS NISAR GCOV visualization layer (8-bit false-color, zoom 12). In the 21 compared overpasses, both radar measurements differ by an average of only 3.58%, well within the physical uncertainty envelope.

- Physical Uncertainty Quantification: Rather than arbitrary percentage margins, uncertainty bounds (area_min and area_max) are physically computed by evaluating pixel-level morphological connectivity across ±12% intensity threshold variations.

- High-Performance Web Mapping: Built with MapLibre GL JS consuming NASA GIBS WMTS raster tiles (NISAR L2 GCOV and VIIRS TrueColor). It features an interactive "Cloud Curtain" split-screen swipe tool, allowing users to physically drag a divider revealing thick white optical clouds on the left and crisp radar-pierced reservoir water on the right.

### 4. Ground-Truth Agreement, Orbit Decoupling & Statistical Robustness

We evaluated 21 NISAR overpasses (June to November 2026) against official daily reservoir useful volume percentages reported by XM Sinergox (Colombia’s national grid and wholesale energy/water market operator):

- Primary Method (Level-2 GCOV γ⁰ in dB):

* Combined Integrated Series: ρ = 0.9831 (p = 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁵, n = 21, mean area = 5.216 km²)

* Descending Track 083: ρ = 0.9636 (p = 1.85 × 10⁻⁶, n = 11, mean area = 5.206 km²)

* Ascending Track 119: ρ = 0.9879 (p = 9.31 × 10⁻⁸, n = 10, mean area = 5.227 km²)

- Comparison Series (NASA GIBS 8-bit tiles):

* Combined: ρ = 0.7935 (p = 1.77 × 10⁻⁵, n = 21, mean area = 5.116 km²)

Rigorous Statistical Validation & Absence of Systematic Orbit Bias:

1. Paired Orbit Test: When pairing consecutive passes (Δt ≤ 3 days, n = 10 pairs), the mean paired difference between Descending 083 and Ascending 119 is -0.0061 km² (-0.1%), with a Wilcoxon p = 0.3887 and paired t-test p = 0.6287. The 95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.0282, +0.0171] km² includes zero, confirming that there is NO statistically significant systematic bias between orbits. Unverified hypotheses (catabatic winds, foreshortening) are noted as hypotheses without in situ anemometers.

2. Temporal Autocorrelation & Detrending: Under a block bootstrap preserving serial dependence, the 95% confidence interval remains strictly positive [0.8501, 0.9961]. Furthermore, step-by-step first-differences (ΔArea vs ΔXM) achieve ρ = 0.7880 (p = 3.7 × 10⁻⁵), and quadratic detrended residuals achieve ρ = 0.8390 (p = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶), proving that while the macro-filling trend accounts for baseline covariance, the radar dynamically captures real incremental volume fluctuations.

### 5. Scalability & Transferability

Submitted through the virtual local event of Ipiales and developed in Bogotá for the strategic reservoirs supplying the capital, 'Ojo de Agua' establishes a lightweight, transferable blueprint. The exact same workflow can be applied to monitor high-altitude Andean lakes in Nariño (such as La Cocha Lagoon), reservoirs across Ecuador and Peru, or any cloud-impacted freshwater basin globally.
